question: What techniques make diffusion model sampling faster?
sub_questions: What numerical solvers and ODE/SDE integration schemes reduce the number of function evaluations needed for diffusion model sampling?
How do distillation and consistency-based methods compress multi-step diffusion sampling into few or single steps?
How do architectural and latent-space modifications, such as latent diffusion and efficient network designs, reduce the per-step computational cost of diffusion sampling?
report:
# Techniques for Faster Diffusion Model Sampling: A Literature Review

## Introduction

Diffusion models generate high-quality samples but classically need hundreds or thousands of sequential network evaluations. The literature attacks this cost along three axes. The first is better numerical solvers, which cut the number of function evaluations (NFE) without retraining. The second is distillation and consistency training, which compress the trajectory into a few steps or one. The third is architectural and latent-space design, which lowers the cost of each step. This review covers each axis and notes where the evidence is thin.

## Better solvers for the reverse process

Sampling can be cast as solving a reverse-time SDE or its probability-flow ODE, and a predictor-corrector scheme was proposed early to correct discretization error [2011.13456]. DDIM defined a deterministic, non-Markovian sampler that is 10× to 50× faster than DDPM in wall-clock time [2010.02502]. gDDIM reinterpreted DDIM as a particular score approximation for the SDE and extended it to non-isotropic diffusions, reporting FID 2.26 at 50 NFE on CIFAR-10 [2206.05564].

High-order ODE solvers pushed step counts lower. DPM-Solver computes the linear part of the ODE solution analytically and applies a high-order solver to the rest, reporting FID 4.70 at 10 NFE and 2.87 at 20 NFE on CIFAR-10 [2206.00927]. DPM-Solver++ adds a data-prediction formulation and thresholding for guided sampling, and reports needing 15–20 steps for guided sampling [2211.01095]. PNDM treats DDPM as solving differential equations on manifolds, shows DDIM is a special case, and reports that 50 steps give better quality than 1000-step DDIM [2202.09778]. UniPC adds a corrector (UniC) that raises the order after any existing sampler without extra evaluations, plus a predictor (UniP), reaching FID 3.87 at 10 NFE on CIFAR-10 [2302.04867]. Karras et al. separated sampler, training, and preconditioning choices, reaching FID 1.97 on unconditional CIFAR-10 with 35 network evaluations per image, and they improved pretrained models without retraining [2206.00364].

Recent training-free work takes other routes. FSampler extrapolates the epsilon prediction from recent history to skip model calls, cutting calls by 15–25% at high fidelity and up to 45–50% at lower fidelity [2511.09180]. CHORDS parallelises several solvers across cores, reporting up to 2.9× speedup with eight cores [2507.15260].

## Distillation and consistency methods

Solvers reach good quality around 10 steps, whereas distillation targets 1–4 steps. Progressive distillation trains a student to match a many-step deterministic teacher in half as many steps and repeats the halving. It reaches FID 3.0 on CIFAR-10 at 4 steps, from teachers that used up to 8192 steps [2202.00512].

Consistency models map any point on a trajectory directly to the data, so one step suffices by design, while multistep sampling remains available to trade compute for quality. They can be distilled from a pretrained diffusion model or trained standalone, and reach one-step FID 3.55 on CIFAR-10 and 6.20 on ImageNet 64x64 [2303.01469]. Bidirectional Consistency Models learn both forward and backward traversal of the probability-flow ODE, which enables inversion as well as generation [2403.18035]. Phased Consistency Models report design flaws in latent consistency models at high resolution and with text conditioning, and generalize the design to 1–16 steps [2405.18407]. That description of latent consistency models is secondhand, since the original paper is not among the sources here.

Adversarial and score-based distillation target large text-to-image models. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation combines score distillation with an adversarial loss to reach 1–4 steps [2311.17042]. LADD moves the discriminator into latent space and yields SD3-Turbo with four unguided steps [2403.12015]. SDXL-Lightning combines progressive and adversarial distillation for 1024px generation [2402.13929]. Score Implicit Matching distills into a single-step generator without training data, reporting FID 2.06 on unconditional CIFAR-10 [2410.16794].

## Reducing per-step cost

A third family makes each evaluation cheaper. Latent diffusion runs diffusion in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder, which significantly reduces computational requirements relative to pixel space [2112.10752]. The mechanism is that each denoising call operates on a much smaller tensor, although the abstract gives no per-step FLOP breakdown. Latent diffusion does not itself reduce step count. That is a separate axis, as Improved DDPM shows, where learned variances allow sampling with an order of magnitude fewer forward passes [2102.09672].

Architecture makes per-step cost an explicit design variable. Diffusion Transformers operate on latent patches and measure cost in forward-pass Gflops, finding that quality tracks Gflops, which can be raised through depth, width, or token count [2212.09748]. At inference, token-reduction methods cut compute further. Token Fusion combines pruning and merging and reports gains on classification and image generation [2312.01026]. ClusCa, a training-free method for diffusion transformers, clusters tokens at each timestep and computes one token per cluster. It reports over 90% fewer tokens and 4.96× acceleration on FLUX [2509.10312].

## Open problems

Several gaps remain. The distillation papers make individual claims but are not compared head-to-head on a shared benchmark, and no unified theory explains why the methods differ. The solver evidence is concentrated in 2022–2023 work on CIFAR-10, so how well those gains carry over to modern large models is only partly tested. For per-step cost, I found no study directly quantifying the savings of latent versus pixel diffusion, and no U-Net-specific efficient-design analysis. Finally, the axes are rarely combined systematically. It is unclear how much solver, distillation, and token-reduction gains compound, or where they interfere.
